items.title: Time and work — the units (LCM) method
items.body:
### Time and work — the units (LCM) method

**The idea in one sentence**
Instead of juggling fractions, call the whole job a convenient number of units so each worker's daily output is a whole number, then simply add or subtract units.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
A finishes a job in 18 days, B in 9 days; B works 3 days then leaves and A finishes the rest — how long does A take? Pick a job size both day-values divide into: 18 works for both 18 and 9, so let the job be 18 units. Then A does 18 ÷ 18 = 1 unit a day and B does 18 ÷ 9 = 2 units a day. In 3 days B completes 3 × 2 = 6 units, leaving 18 − 6 = 12 units. A clears those at 1 unit a day, so A needs 12 days. No fractions appeared, because the clever job size made every rate a whole number.

**Why pick the LCM as the job size?**
The lowest common multiple of the given days is the smallest number every day-value divides exactly, so each rate (job ÷ days) comes out whole and the arithmetic stays clean.

```
 job = 18 units | A = 1/day | B = 2/day
 B: 3 days -> 6 units ; left 12 -> A takes 12 days
```

**What the symbols mean**
- rate means how much of the job someone finishes in one day.
- unit means one equal share of the whole job after you set the job size.
- LCM means the lowest common multiple, the smallest number the given day-values all divide.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Rate = 1 ÷ (days alone). Two people together take 1 ÷ (1/a + 1/b) days, which also equals a × b ÷ (a + b). If one person is k times as efficient as another, their rate ratio is k to 1 and their days ratio is 1 to k, so the faster one takes fewer days.

**Exam-level example**
A does a job in 12 days and B in 15 days; together how long? Rates 1/12 and 1/15 add to 5/60 + 4/60 = 9/60 = 3/20 of the job per day, so time = 20 ÷ 3 = 6 and two-thirds days. Check with the product rule: a × b ÷ (a + b) = 12 × 15 ÷ 27 = 180 ÷ 27 = 6 and two-thirds days — the same answer.

**Common traps**
- Adding the days (12 + 15) for combined work; days never add, rates do.
- Taking the plain average of the two times, which is always too large.
- Forgetting that the more efficient worker needs fewer days, not more.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| job = LCM of days | makes every daily rate a whole number |
| together = a×b ÷ (a+b) | time for two working together |
| k times efficient | days ratio is 1 to k |
keyPoints: Rate of work = 1 ÷ (days to finish alone); work done = rate × time.
Units method: set the job = LCM of the days so every rate is a whole number of units a day.
Together time = a × b ÷ (a + b) = 1 ÷ (1/a + 1/b).
k times as efficient means a rate ratio of k to 1 and a days ratio of 1 to k.
Never add the individual days for combined work.
items.mnemonic: Think units, not fractions — the LCM turns every rate into a clean whole number.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Fractions of Work / Efficiency and Work Comparison

items.title: Alternate-days work
items.body:
### Alternate-days work

**The idea in one sentence**
When two people work on alternate days, add up one full two-day cycle, fit as many whole cycles as you can, then finish the small leftover with whoever's turn is next.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
A finishes a job in 8 days, B in 12 days, and they work alternate days with A starting. Make the job LCM(8, 12) = 24 units, so A does 3 units a day and B does 2 units a day. Day 1 (A): 3 units. Day 2 (B): 2 more, total 5. So each A-then-B pair clears 5 units. Four such pairs take 8 days and clear 4 × 5 = 20 units. Day 9 is A's turn: +3 units makes 23. Only 1 unit is left, and day 10 is B's turn at 2 units a day, so B needs just half a day. Total = 9 and a half days.

**Why might the last person need only part of a day?**
Work ends the moment the units run out, which usually happens partway through someone's day, so you divide the leftover units by that person's daily rate instead of rounding up to a full day.

```
 cycle = A(3) + B(2) = 5 units per 2 days
 4 cycles -> 20 (8 days) ; +A 3 -> 23 ; +B needs 1/2 day
```

**What the symbols mean**
- cycle means one full round of turns, here A's day plus B's day.
- leftover means the units still unfinished after the last whole cycle.
- rate means the units done in one day by that person.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Units per cycle = sum of the two daily rates. Whole cycles = the largest number of cycles that stays at or below the job. Remaining time = leftover units ÷ (the next person's daily rate). Add the whole-cycle days to that final part of a day.

**Exam-level example**
A (3 units/day) and B (2 units/day) on a 24-unit job, A first: 4 cycles clear 20 units in 8 days; A's 9th day adds 3 to reach 23; B clears the last 1 unit in 1 ÷ 2 = half a day, giving 9 and a half days. Check: A works days 1,3,5,7,9 (5 × 3 = 15 units) and B works days 2,4,6,8 plus half of day 10 (4 × 2 + 1 = 9 units); 15 + 9 = 24 units.

**Common traps**
- Rounding the last person's part-day up to a whole day.
- Forgetting that who starts first changes the leftover.
- Not setting the job to the LCM, so the daily rates are not whole numbers.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| cycle = rateA + rateB | work done in one A-then-B round |
| whole cycles first | fit as many full rounds as possible |
| leftover ÷ next rate | the final part-day |
keyPoints: Alternate work: add one full cycle (A's day + B's day) first.
Fit whole cycles, then finish the leftover with the next person's turn.
The final stretch is often a fraction of a day — do not round it up automatically.
Who starts first matters when the work finishes mid-cycle.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Alternate Days Work

items.title: Work and wages, and the man-days rule
items.body:
### Work and wages, and the man-days rule

**The idea in one sentence**
Pay is shared in proportion to the work each person actually does, and for one fixed job the product of workers, days and daily hours stays constant.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
A finishes a job in 6 days and B in 8 days; together they are paid 2800 rupees — what is A's share? In one day A does one-sixth of the job and B does one-eighth. Compare the two on a common footing: one-sixth versus one-eighth is the same as 4 twenty-fourths versus 3 twenty-fourths, so A and B do work in the ratio 4 to 3. Split 2800 rupees into 4 + 3 = 7 equal parts of 400 rupees each: A gets 4 × 400 = 1600 rupees and B gets 3 × 400 = 1200 rupees. The faster worker did more of the job, so earns more.

**Why does pay follow work done, not days spent?**
Wages reward output. Someone who completes a bigger slice of the job has earned a bigger slice of the money, which is why the faster, more efficient worker takes the larger share.

```
 A:B work = 1/6 : 1/8 = 4 : 3 ; 2800 ÷ 7 = 400 ; A = 1600, B = 1200
```

**What the symbols mean**
- M means the number of workers (men).
- D means the number of days.
- H means the hours worked each day.
- W means the amount of work; keep it in the ratio only when the job size changes.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Wages are split in the ratio of the workers' rates. For the same job, M × D × H is constant, so M1 × D1 × H1 = M2 × D2 × H2. If the job size also changes, compare (M × D × H) ÷ W on each side.

**Exam-level example**
10 men working 8 hours a day finish a job in 6 days; how many days will 8 men working 10 hours a day need? Keep M × D × H constant: 10 × 8 × 6 = 8 × 10 × D, so 480 = 80 × D and D = 6 days. Check: the first team supplies 480 man-hours; the second supplies 8 × 10 = 80 man-hours a day, and 480 ÷ 80 = 6 days.

**Common traps**
- Dropping the hours term, so fewer men looks like it needs more days when longer hours offset them.
- Splitting wages equally when the efficiencies differ.
- Giving the larger wage to the slower worker.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| wage ratio = rate ratio | the faster worker earns more |
| M×D×H constant | same job: trade men for hours or days |
| compare ÷ W | use this when the job size changes |
keyPoints: Wages are shared in the ratio of work done, which equals the ratio of efficiency (1/a : 1/b).
The faster worker (fewer days) earns the larger share.
M1 × D1 × H1 = M2 × D2 × H2 for the same amount of work.
Include the work amount W in the ratio when the job size changes.
items.mnemonic: M × D × H stays constant — more men or hours means fewer days.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Work and Wages / Man-Hours Concept

items.title: Pipes and cisterns
items.body:
### Pipes and cisterns

**The idea in one sentence**
A pipe filling a tank is a worker doing positive work and a pipe draining it is a worker doing negative work, so you add inlet rates and subtract outlet rates.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B in 4 hours; both open together take how long? In one hour A fills one-sixth of the tank and B fills one-quarter. Put them over a common bottom of 12: one-sixth is 2 twelfths and one-quarter is 3 twelfths, so together they fill 2 + 3 = 5 twelfths of the tank each hour. To fill the whole tank (12 twelfths) at 5 twelfths an hour takes 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 hours, which is 2 hours 24 minutes. You only added the two one-hour shares.

**Why subtract an outlet instead of adding it?**
An outlet removes water, the opposite of filling, so its hourly share counts as a negative amount; the tank only fills when the inlets together beat the outlets.

```
 inlets +1/6 +1/4 = +5/12 per hour -> fill in 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 h
 inlet 1/10 minus outlet 1/15 = +1/30 per hour -> 30 h
```

**What the symbols mean**
- inlet means a pipe that fills, counted as positive.
- outlet or leak means a pipe that empties, counted as negative.
- net rate means the amount of tank filled per hour after combining all pipes.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Net rate = sum of inlet rates − sum of outlet rates. Fill time = 1 ÷ net rate. The tank fills only when the net rate is positive. Two inlets a and b together take a × b ÷ (a + b) hours.

**Exam-level example**
An inlet fills a tank in 10 hours while an outlet empties a full tank in 15 hours; both open on an empty tank take how long? Net rate = 1/10 − 1/15 = 3/30 − 2/30 = 1/30 of the tank per hour, which is positive, so it fills in 30 hours. Check: in 30 hours the inlet alone would fill 3 tanks and the outlet would drain 2, leaving exactly 1 tank filled.

**Common traps**
- Adding the outlet instead of subtracting it.
- Concluding the tank fills when the outlet is actually faster (a negative net rate).
- Adding the two times (10 + 15) instead of combining the rates.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| net = inlets − outlets | combine all pipes per hour |
| time = 1 ÷ net | hours to fill |
| fills only when net is positive | inlets must beat outlets |
keyPoints: An inlet rate is added (positive); an outlet or leak rate is subtracted (negative).
Fill time = 1 ÷ net rate; the tank fills only when the net rate is positive.
Two inlets together take a × b ÷ (a + b) hours.
A leak that empties in y hours lowers the effective rate by 1/y.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Pipes and Cistern

items.title: Speed, distance, time and trains
items.body:
### Speed, distance, time and trains

**The idea in one sentence**
Distance equals speed times time, and most train questions are just this one rule once you choose the right distance to cover and the right relative speed.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
A 150 m train runs at 54 km/h and crosses a 210 m platform — how long? First change the speed to metres per second so it matches the lengths: 54 km/h means 54 × 1000 metres in 3600 seconds, which is 54000 ÷ 3600 = 15 m/s. The front of the train must travel the whole platform plus the whole train before the train is clear: 210 + 150 = 360 m. At 15 m every second, that takes 360 ÷ 15 = 24 seconds. Each step was simply distance = speed × time, rearranged to time = distance ÷ speed.

**Why add both lengths for a platform?**
The train has fully crossed only when its tail leaves the far end, so the front travels the platform length plus the train's own length — add both.

```
 54 km/h = 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s
 distance = platform 210 + train 150 = 360 ; time = 360 ÷ 15 = 24 s
```

**What the symbols mean**
- relative speed means how fast one object closes on another.
- same direction means subtract the speeds; opposite directions means add them.
- 5/18 is the fixed number that turns km/h into m/s (and 18/5 does the reverse).

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Change km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18. Average speed over equal distances = 2 × x × y ÷ (x + y), always smaller than the plain average. For crossings: a pole or person needs just the train length; a platform needs train + platform length; another train needs the sum of both lengths divided by the relative speed (sum of speeds if opposite, difference if same direction).

**Exam-level example**
Two trains 120 m and 180 m long move towards each other at 40 and 50 km/h — how long to cross? Opposite directions, so relative speed = 40 + 50 = 90 km/h = 90 × 5/18 = 25 m/s. Together they must clear 120 + 180 = 300 m, taking 300 ÷ 25 = 12 seconds. Check: at 25 m/s, 12 seconds covers 300 m, exactly both lengths.

**Common traps**
- Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s before dividing by seconds.
- Using the plain average of two speeds instead of 2xy ÷ (x + y) for equal distances.
- Adding speeds for same-direction motion, or subtracting them for opposite directions.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| km/h × 5/18 | changes to metres per second |
| platform: train + platform | distance to fully cross |
| opposite: add, same: subtract | the relative-speed rule |
keyPoints: Convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18; m/s to km/h by multiplying by 18/5.
Average speed for equal distances = 2 × x × y ÷ (x + y), not the plain average.
Same direction means relative speed is the difference; opposite means the sum.
Crossing a pole or person uses the train length; a platform adds the platform length; another train adds both lengths.
Early or late: distance ÷ v1 − distance ÷ v2 = the total time gap in hours.
items.mnemonic: 5/18 to go down to m/s, 18/5 to go up; same direction subtract, opposite add.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Average Speed / Relative speed / Problem on Train

items.title: Boats and streams, and races
items.body:
### Boats and streams, and races

**The idea in one sentence**
A stream speeds a boat up going downstream and slows it by the same amount going upstream, and a race 'beats by' tells you how far the loser got while the winner finished.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
A boat does 30 km downstream in 2 hours and the same 30 km upstream in 3 hours; find the boat's own speed and the stream's. Downstream speed = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 km/h; upstream speed = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 km/h. Downstream is boat plus stream and upstream is boat minus stream, so their average removes the stream: boat = (15 + 10) ÷ 2 = 12.5 km/h, and half their gap is the stream = (15 − 10) ÷ 2 = 2.5 km/h. Quick check: 12.5 + 2.5 = 15 (downstream) and 12.5 − 2.5 = 10 (upstream), both correct.

**Why does averaging give the boat's own speed?**
Downstream carries one extra stream-speed and upstream loses one stream-speed, so averaging the two cancels the stream and leaves the boat alone; half their difference is the stream.

```
 down = boat + stream = 15 ; up = boat - stream = 10
 boat = (15+10) ÷ 2 = 12.5 ; stream = (15-10) ÷ 2 = 2.5
```

**What the symbols mean**
- B means the boat's speed in still water.
- S means the stream's (current's) speed.
- 'beats by d metres' means the winner finishes while the loser is still d metres short.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Downstream speed = B + S; upstream speed = B − S. Recover them with B = (down + up) ÷ 2 and S = (down − up) ÷ 2. In an L-metre race, if A beats B by d metres then in equal time A runs L while B runs L − d, so the speed ratio is L to (L − d). A 'start of x metres' means the opponent runs only L − x.

**Exam-level example**
In a 100 m race A beats B by 20 metres; what is the speed ratio A to B? While A runs the full 100 m, B runs only 100 − 20 = 80 m in the same time, and equal time means speed is proportional to distance, so A to B = 100 : 80 = 5 : 4. Check: if A's speed is 5 units and B's is 4, then in the time A covers 100 m, B covers 80 m — a 20 m gap, exactly as given.

**Common traps**
- Swapping downstream and upstream; downstream is always the faster one.
- Forgetting that upstream is the slower effective speed when solving for time.
- Reading 'beats by 20 m' as B's total distance instead of the gap.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| down = B + S, up = B − S | stream adds going down, subtracts going up |
| B = (down + up) ÷ 2 | averaging cancels the stream |
| beats by d in an L race | speed ratio is L to (L − d) |
keyPoints: Downstream speed = B + S; upstream speed = B − S.
Boat speed = (down + up) ÷ 2; stream speed = (down − up) ÷ 2.
Upstream is always the slower (smaller) effective speed.
Beaten by d metres in an L-metre race means a speed ratio of L to (L − d).
A start of x metres means the opponent runs only L − x.
items.mnemonic: Down adds, up subtracts; boat is the average of the two speeds, stream is half their gap.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Boat and Stream / Race

items.title: Men, women and boys equivalence
items.body:
### Men, women and boys equivalence

**The idea in one sentence**
When a problem says one type of worker equals another (two men equal three women), first turn everybody into one single type, then use the ordinary man-days counting.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Two men do as much as three women; 6 men and 6 women finish a job in 8 days — how long would 12 women alone take? Convert the men to women first. If 2 men = 3 women then 1 man = 1.5 women, so 6 men = 9 women. The team of 6 men and 6 women is therefore 9 + 6 = 15 women. In 8 days 15 women finish the job, so the whole job is 15 × 8 = 120 woman-days of work. Now 12 women share those 120 woman-days: 120 ÷ 12 = 10 days. Every step used one currency — women — so the counting stayed simple.

**Why convert before counting?**
A man-count and a woman-count are different currencies with different outputs; adding them directly is like adding rupees to dollars. The given equivalence is the exchange rate that makes them comparable.

```
 2 men = 3 women -> 1 man = 1.5 women -> 6 men = 9 women
 team = 9 + 6 = 15 women ; work = 15 × 8 = 120 woman-days
 12 women -> 120 ÷ 12 = 10 days
```

**What the symbols mean**
- equivalence means the given swap rate between worker types.
- worker-days means workers multiplied by days, a measure of total work.
- common unit means the single worker type you convert everyone into.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Use the equivalence to express all workers in one type. Total work = (equivalent workers) × days, and this stays constant for the same job. Divide that total by the new equivalent workforce to get the new time. Handy special case: two teams that each finish in the same time t together take t ÷ 2, because their rates add.

**Exam-level example**
4 men finish a job in 12 days and 6 women finish the same job in 12 days; how long do 4 men and 6 women together take? Each group alone does 1/12 of the job per day, so together they do 1/12 + 1/12 = 2/12 = 1/6 per day, which means 6 days. Check: two equal 12-day teams working together must halve the time, and 12 ÷ 2 = 6 days.

**Common traps**
- Adding men and women directly before converting them.
- Forgetting that total worker-days is constant for the same job.
- Mixing up which type the equivalence converts into which.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| convert to one type | use the given swap rate first |
| work = workers × days | total worker-days, which is constant |
| two equal teams | together take half the time |
keyPoints: Convert all worker types to one common unit using the given equivalence (for example 2 men = 3 women).
Total work in worker-days = equivalent workers × days, and it is constant for the same job.
Two teams that each finish in time t together take t ÷ 2 (rates add).
Do not add different worker types before converting them.
items.mnemonic: One currency first — convert men, women and boys before you count days.
